quotes.text: In the household matrix approach, information is obtained on the relationship between each pair of household members, and a matrix of relationships is produced from which the number and composition of families and households can be derived automatically.

An extended family includes all people within a household who are related in some way: partners; parents; children; grandparents; grandchildren; brothers and sisters; relatives by marriage; guardians; and other relatives.

A household is defined as a single person, or a group of people living at the same address who have the address as their only or main residence and either share one main meal a day or share the living accommodation (or both).

A LFS family unit comprises either a single person, or a married or cohabiting couple on their own, or with their never-married children who have no children of their own, or lone parents with such children.
In most cases the household and the family unit are the same, but it is not uncommon for a household to contain more than one family unit.

assessments.reasoning:
The supplied documentation establishes the following for each element:
- member_to_member_relationships: The questionnaire (question R) and methodological notes confirm that relationships are collected member-to-member between each pair of household members via a household matrix ("Code relationship of [Name] to [Name]").
- extended_ties: Question R lists explicit categories including cohabiting partner, civil partner, step/foster relationships, parents-in-law, siblings, grandchildren, grandparents, other relatives, and non-relatives.
- multiple_household_criteria: The technical manual explicitly defines household criteria based on living at the same address as main residence and sharing one main meal a day or living accommodation (or both).
- sub_units: The technical manual defines LFS family units and establishes that households can contain secondary families or sub-units ("not uncommon for a household to contain more than one family unit").
- caregiving_relationships: While questions such as NOLWF and REDYRS record whether caring for children or adults is a reason for not seeking work or leaving a job, the instrument does not record dyadic caregiving relationships identifying who specifically provides care to whom.
